claims.text: Increasing chemical short-range order enhances electron–phonon coupling in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling caused by short-range order raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Local chemical ordering has a more dominant influence on superconductivity than disorder-induced electron scattering.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase superconducting high-entropy alloy.
The as-cast starting state is chemically disordered.
Rapid quenching preserves a highly disordered chemical state.
Slow annealing promotes chemical short-range order without changing the alloy's overall composition.
The degree of chemical short-range order can be quantified using diffuse X-ray scattering or local-probe methods.
Partial chemical ordering modifies the phonon spectrum.
The phonon-spectrum modification produced by ordering enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling counteracts the effects of disorder-induced electron scattering.
Slow-annealed, more ordered samples will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-annealed samples will exhibit a sharper superconducting-gap signature than rapidly quenched samples.
The rapidly quenched baseline retains maximal chemical disorder.
Electron scattering in the rapidly quenched baseline limits its electron–phonon coupling strength.
The proposed mechanism applies to fixed-composition high-entropy alloys that already exhibit superconductivity under cryogenic, low-field conditions.
The ordering effect may differ for markedly different alloy compositions or outside the superconducting regime.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that all measurements are performed at temperatures below T_c, but determining a superconducting transition temperature by resistivity or susceptibility requires measurements spanning the transition, including temperatures at or above T_c.
